brief.situation: 02:10 on a surgical unit. The central monitor alarms: Mr. Hutchins in Room 9, 61, has an SpO2 of 85% on 2 L by nasal cannula. He had an open colectomy at 14:00 and has a hydromorphone PCA. His wife, staying overnight, says she 'pressed the button for him a few times so he could sleep'.
handover: Obstructive sleep apnea (his CPAP machine is at home), BMI 38, no opioids before surgery. Gabapentin 300 mg at 21:00.
PCA: hydromorphone 0.2 mg per demand, 10-minute lockout, no basal rate. At 00:00 he was easy to rouse, RR 16, SpO2 95%.
Orders: naloxone 0.1 mg IV every 2-3 minutes as needed for POSS 4 or RR below 8, titrated to response; notify the surgical resident for POSS 3 or 4. Policy: sedation and RR with every PCA check.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Recognize, act, then keep evaluating: what you give works for a while, and the plan may have to change.
Partway through you are asked to write what you think is happening. The case ends at 03:40, then a debrief scores what you did.

cues.question: Map what you did onto clinical judgment: what cues, what is happening, what you did, how you are evaluating it, and whether the pain plan continues, changes or ends.

parts.label: Cues and hypothesis
parts.criteria: Names POSS 4 (barely rousable), slow shallow breathing with pauses, SpO2 85%, and his risk factors (untreated sleep apnea, obesity, opioid-naive, gabapentin, PCA by proxy) as opioid-induced respiratory depression; not 'catching up on sleep'.
parts.modelAnswer: POSS 4 with RR 7, snoring with pauses and an SpO2 of 85% is opioid-induced respiratory depression. Sleep apnea without his CPAP, a BMI of 38, being opioid-naive, gabapentin, and his wife pressing the PCA all raised his risk.

parts.label: Action, evaluation and the plan
parts.criteria: Stops the PCA and rouses him first, opens the airway, gives naloxone 0.1 mg every 2-3 minutes to effect rather than 0.4 mg at once, puts him on continuous capnography, takes the button from his wife, escalates to the resident asking for the plan to change; evaluates again at least 30 minutes after naloxone because it wears off before hydromorphone; does not restart the PCA or leave him.
parts.modelAnswer: Stop the PCA, rouse him, head up and airway open, then naloxone 0.1 mg, repeated at 2 minutes to effect, not 0.4 mg pushed. Capnography on, the button out of his wife's hand, and an SBAR to the resident asking to stop the PCA and change to non-opioid relief with CPAP. Evaluation decides the plan: naloxone's half-life is about an hour and hydromorphone's over two, so I reassess at 30 minutes and after, give more if he drifts off, and the old PCA plan ends.

noProgress.rationale: Still drifting off with slow breathing (POSS 3 or worse) 90 minutes after the alarm means an hour and a half of hypoventilation in a man with sleep apnea: this case calls that harm.

reasoningCriteria.label: Written reasoning: the cues, the hypothesis, and evaluation deciding the plan

expertPath.text: Rouse him: POSS 4. Pause the PCA, take the button from his wife, head up and airway open, count RR for a full minute: 7.
Naloxone 0.1 mg IV; again at 2 minutes. Capnography on. He rouses: POSS 2, RR 14.
SBAR to the resident: oversedated on the PCA, high risk, naloxone may wear off; please stop the PCA and change the plan.
New orders: PCA off, IV acetaminophen, capnography, CPAP. Explain to his wife; objective note.
Reassess at 30 minutes and after; when he drifts toward POSS 3 again, another 0.1 mg.

arrest.headline: He stopped breathing
arrest.body: POSS 4 with RR 7 means stop the opioid now and consider naloxone. Find when the PCA was paused, who held the button, and when the first naloxone went in.

stillSedated.headline: Breathing too little for too long
stillSedated.body: Stopping the PCA alone lets hydromorphone wear off over hours. POSS 4 with slow breathing needs naloxone to effect and a resident who changes the plan.

safe.headline: Reversed, watched, plan changed
safe.body: You stopped the drug, reversed it in small doses so his pain relief was not torn away, watched past the point naloxone wears off, and used that evaluation to end the PCA plan. That is the expert path.

safeLate.headline: Breathing, by a slower route
safeLate.body: He is breathing, but check how fast the PCA stopped, the naloxone dose, who gave it, whether he was watched past 30 minutes, and whether the plan changed.

time_up.body: The case ran to its hard stop.

scoring.modelReasoning: Recognize: POSS 4 (barely rousable), RR 7 with pauses, SpO2 85%. Analyze and prioritize: opioid-induced respiratory depression in a man with untreated sleep apnea, obesity, no opioid tolerance and gabapentin, made worse by his wife pressing the PCA. Act: pause the PCA, rouse him, head up and airway open, and give naloxone 0.1 mg IV every 2-3 minutes to effect (a full 0.4 mg push tears away his analgesia and can cause vomiting, tachycardia, hypertension and worse). Put him on continuous capnography; more oxygen alone only hides the problem. Escalate to the resident with an SBAR that asks for the plan to change. Evaluate: naloxone's half-life is 30-81 minutes and hydromorphone's about 2.3 hours, so reassess at 30 minutes and after and repeat naloxone if he drifts off. The evaluation ends the PCA plan: non-opioid analgesia, CPAP, monitoring, and teaching his wife that only he presses the button.
